 Huge veterinary compounding recall causes scramble 
 Veterinarians reported supply interruptions prior to recall announcement
 Published: November 06, 2026 
 By 
 Lena Beck 
 Series 
 See related stories » 
 pills_falling_recalled.jpg 
 Art by Tamara Rees 
 Shortly after waking up on a recent morning, Dr. Brandie Cox was checking the news on her phone when she saw something that stopped her mid-scroll: A new veterinary medication recall was underway that involved nearly 4,000 items, counting separate lots and expiration dates.
 Cox hurriedly clicked the link and learned that the recall was issued by Wedgewood Pharmacy, a leading compounding pharmacy for veterinary medications in the United States.
 "I was, frankly, mortified," Cox said. "We use them for almost all of our compounding needs, and I've specifically picked them for accuracy and their high level of certification."
 The Oct. 21  recall notice  cited the issue as "inconsistencies in the reliability of certain analytical testing data generated by their laboratory," potentially resulting in medication that was too strong or not strong enough.
 Compounding involves customizing medication — such as by dose, flavoring or form — to meet the needs of individual patients. The role of compounding in veterinary medicine is expansive, in part because there are not animal drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for all species and indications. Compounded preparations are not approved by the FDA like conventional drugs.
 Wedgewood Pharmacy, founded in 1981 and headquartered in New Jersey, serves more than 70,000 veterinarians and one million animals each year, according to the company website .
 In brief 
 * A recall of nearly 4,000 product listings by Wedgewood Pharmacy, a leading veterinary compounder, set off a scramble among veterinarians and pet owners.
 * Wedgewood initiated the voluntary recall, announced Oct. 21, after detecting inconsistency in the analytical data used to evaluate product potency.
 * Before the recall, Wedgewood stopped sales of some products, leading to confusion among veterinarian customers.
 * Wedgewood has retained Sedgwick, a company that manages product recalls, to coordinate customer notifications and refunds.
 Based in Texas, Cox is one of their customers. A solo small animal practitioner, she said she had 51 patients, of her total client base of around 2,000, on medications from Wedgewood. The preparations she ordered from the pharmacy included ophthalmic cyclosporine solution, for dry eyes; pimobendan, a heart medication; and intravenous buprenorphine, used for pain management.
 "I'll be honest, I'm never going to use them again," Cox said of the pharmacy. "I'm sitting here this afternoon, with time I don't have, going through every single client that uses them. And we're going to find an alternative source ... because my trust has been completely destroyed in them."
 Cox's concerns were echoed on a message board of the Veterinary Information Network, an online community for the profession and parent of the VIN News Service. Veterinarians there recounted interruptions in supply, described their efforts to chase down and replace affected medications, and expressed frustration at how the recall is being handled.
 Uncertainty preceding the recall 
 The nearly 4,000 items on the recall list was eye-catching in scope. But Dr. Rae Hutchins, Wedgewood chief veterinary officer, told VIN News by email that the number encompasses variations in products, such as different expiration dates or lot numbers and is not a tally of distinct medications affected. She also said that not every item on the list definitively was found to be too weak or too strong, but rather, Wedgewood's internal quality checks found inconsistencies in its testing data that caused the company to be uncertain that the medications met potency requirements.
 "As the investigation progressed, we determined that voluntarily recalling the affected products within expiry was the responsible course of action," Hutchins said.
 According to the recall notice, Wedgewood has received 98 complaints, seven of them serious. "The health risks involved with low potency can include ineffective treatment, and the health risks involved with high potency can include toxicity or overdose," the notice said.
 In the days leading up to the recall, multiple veterinarians posting on VIN  message boards expressed difficulty obtaining Wedgewood medications. The lack of a clear explanation about the cause resulted in confusion and speculation.
 Hutchins confirmed that the company paused the availability of certain medications in the weeks prior to the recall to stop the distribution of potentially affected medications while it continued to investigate.
 "These were proactive measures intended to prevent additional potentially affected products from reaching veterinary practices and patients while we worked to understand the scope of the issue," she said.
 Hutchins said that once the recall was announced, the large number of affected products, lots and customers meant the notification process took time.
 "We recognize that some veterinarians learned about the recall publicly before receiving their individual notifications, and we understand their frustration," she said.
 What happens now 
 Hutchins said there is not yet a definitive timeline for restoring the availability of all affected product listings. Wedgewood is encouraging its customers to review the recall information on the company's website to identify affected products. The pharmacy has retained Sedgwick, a third-party service, to coordinate the recall. Sedgwick is leading the effort to notify customers and organize refunds or replacements when possible.
 Hutchins said that Wedgewood understands that this experience has been difficult for its customers.
 "For more than 40 years, veterinarians have trusted Wedgewood to help care for animals," she said. "We don't take that trust for granted. We know that rebuilding confidence will require us to demonstrate our commitment through the actions we take moving forward."
